The call sets the book's two directions

Verse 10 gives Jeremiah’s task in six verbs. Four of them tear down: uproot, tear down, destroy, overthrow. Two of them build: build and plant. That proportion matches the book that follows. The tearing down also comes first in the order. A young man from a village is set “over the nations.” These verbs return in 18:7–9, 24:6, and 31:28.
A water image explains failed dependence

Verse 13 counts two wrongs. The people left a spring, and they dug cisterns. A spring flows on its own with fresh water. A cistern is a pit cut in rock to catch runoff. It takes hard labor, and its plaster cracks. So the people gave up a gift for a leaking thing they made. Verse 18 applies the picture to alliances and verses 27–28 to idols.
One nation's failure does not excuse another

Judah watched the northern kingdom fall (2 Kings 17). Verse 8 says she saw it and learned nothing. Verse 10 says her return was “in pretense.” So verse 11 gives a surprising verdict. The nation with more warning is the more guilty. The invitation then goes to the north first (verse 12). Verse 13 sets one condition: “Only acknowledge your iniquity.”
Destruction reverses the language of creation

Verse 23 echoes Genesis 1:2, where the earth was formless and empty. Jeremiah says “I saw” four times in verses 23–26. Light is gone, then mountains, people, birds, and gardens. The list runs creation backward. An invasion is described as the world being unmade. Verse 27 sets a limit on it. The land will be ruined, and it will not be the end.
Knowledge of the law does not explain away injustice

Jeremiah’s first guess in verse 4 is generous. Perhaps the poor do wrong because no one taught them. Verse 5 tests that idea on the educated. The leaders know the LORD’s way, and they have thrown it off. So lack of knowledge is not the cause. Verse 28 shows what this looks like in court. The orphan’s case is not heard, and the needy get no justice.
Reassurance can conceal a wound

Verse 14 uses a medical picture. The people have a serious wound. Their leaders dress it lightly and say all is well. Verse 13 gives the motive, which is gain. Verse 15 adds that they feel no shame. Verse 16 offers real rest on the old paths. The people refuse it in so many words.
A temple can become a false source of safety

Verse 4 quotes a phrase the people repeat three times. They treat the building as a guarantee. Verse 9 lists what they do during the week. It names theft, murder, adultery, false oaths, and other gods. Verse 11 calls the temple a robbers’ den, a hideout where thieves feel safe. Verse 12 points to Shiloh, an earlier holy place that fell (1 Samuel 4). Jesus quotes verse 11 in Matthew 21:13.
Possessing written law does not secure right judgment

Verse 7 says migrating birds know their appointed times. God’s people do not know his requirements. Verse 8 quotes their defense. They have the written law, so they are wise. Jeremiah says the scribes’ handling has made it false. Readers differ on exactly what the scribes did. Verse 9 states the result: they reject the LORD’s word while holding it.
Knowing God receives a practical definition

Verse 23 removes three common grounds for pride. Wisdom, strength, and riches are all set aside. Verse 24 leaves one. A person may boast in understanding and knowing the LORD. The verse then says what that knowledge contains. He acts with loving kindness, justice, and righteousness on the earth. Chapter 22:16 defines knowing God as defending the poor.
Craftsmanship and authority are different claims

Verse 5 lists what the idol cannot do. It cannot speak, and it cannot move. Its worshipers must carry it. A god that depends on its people for transport offers them nothing. So the verse says not to fear it. It can do neither harm nor good. Verses 10 and 12–13 set the living God against it.
The speaker's own community tries to restrict his speech

Anathoth is Jeremiah’s home village (1:1). Verse 21 says its men want him dead. They do not argue with his message. They forbid him to speak it. Verse 19 says he had not known of the plot until God showed him. Chapter 12:6 adds that his own brothers were involved. The first threat to this prophet comes from his neighbors.
A complaint tests the gap between justice and experience

Verse 1 opens like a lawsuit. Jeremiah first grants that the LORD is in the right. Then he argues anyway. His question is the one Job and Psalm 73 ask. God’s reply in verse 5 explains nothing. It says the road ahead is harder. An honest complaint is allowed, and it is answered with preparation.
A close-fitting object represents a broken relationship

A belt is worn close against the body. Verse 11 uses it for the bond God meant to have with his people. They were to be his name, praise, and glory. The picture is closeness, not only obedience. The belt is spoiled by being buried somewhere else. Judah’s ruin is the loss of that closeness. Verse 23 adds that long habit has made change hard.
Competing messages appear during visible scarcity

Jeremiah speaks up for the people in verse 13. Other prophets have told them there will be no sword or famine. He suggests they have been misled. The LORD’s answer in verses 14–16 does not accept that excuse. He did not send those prophets, and their hearers share their end. The promise of “assured peace” comes during a drought anyone can see. Two messages are in the air, and events will show which is true.
The prophet's complaint is part of his service

In 2:13 the LORD called himself a spring of living water. In verse 18 Jeremiah turns that picture against him. He asks whether God will be like a stream that fails. It is a severe charge. God’s answer in verse 19 tells the prophet himself to “return.” Then he repeats the promise made at Jeremiah’s call (1:18–19). The complaint is corrected, and the book still keeps it.
Missing household rituals make coming loss visible

Jeremiah receives three bans. He may not marry (verse 2), mourn (verse 5), or feast (verse 8). His own life becomes a sign of what is coming. The ordinary rites of grief and joy are about to stop for everyone. Verse 5 gives the reason for the second ban. God has withdrawn his peace, kindness, and mercy from this people. Chapter 15:17 shows how lonely this made the prophet.
The tree image allows difficulty within trust

Verse 8 resembles Psalm 1:3 and adds something. Heat comes, and a year of drought comes. Trust does not keep the hard season away. The tree stays green because its roots reach the stream. The shrub in verse 6 cannot even see good when it arrives. Verse 9 then warns that the heart can deceive its owner. A person may be wrong about where his trust lies.
Soft clay presents a future that can change

The clay in verse 4 is still wet and on the wheel. The potter can make it again. Verses 7–10 draw a lesson that works in both directions. A warning can be withdrawn, and so can a promise. Verse 8 gives the first case: a nation turns, and God relents. The people reply in verse 12 that nothing can change. They use hopelessness as a reason to go on as before.
A broken vessel changes the force of the earlier image

Chapter 18 used soft clay that a potter could reshape. This chapter uses a finished jar that has been fired. Verse 11 says a broken jar “can’t be made whole again.” The time for reshaping can pass. Jeremiah acts this out before the nation’s leaders. He does it in the valley where children were burned (verse 5). The place and the audience are part of the message.
Praise and anguish remain in the same voice

Jeremiah is caught between two pains. When he speaks, people mock him (verse 8). When he holds back, verse 9 says a fire burns in his bones. He cannot keep it in. Verses 11–13 then speak with trust and praise. Verses 14–18 curse his birth, as Job did. The book places both in one voice and does not explain the change.
A request for rescue meets a demand for justice

Zedekiah hopes for a rescue like the one in Hezekiah’s day (verse 2). Verse 5 says God’s outstretched hand is now against the city. Verse 12 then speaks to the royal house about its neglected work. A king held court in the morning. He was to rescue the person robbed by a stronger one. The king asks for a wonder and is told to do justice. The city’s safety is tied to the safety of its weakest people.
Royal buildings reveal how power treats workers

Verse 13 accuses Jehoiakim of building with forced, unpaid labor. The law required prompt wages (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15). Verse 15 asks whether cedar panels make a man a king. It then points to his father Josiah. Josiah ate and drank well and still did justice. Verse 16 says he judged the cause of the poor and needy. It adds, “Wasn’t this to know me?”
A prophet's effect on conduct matters

The false prophets claim to know God’s mind. Verse 18 asks who has really stood in his council. Verse 22 gives a test that anyone can apply. A prophet who had stood there would turn people from evil. These prophets do the opposite. Verse 14 says they strengthen the hands of evildoers. Verse 17 says they promise peace to people who despise the LORD.
Remaining at home does not prove divine favor

Those left in Jerusalem thought they were the favored ones (Ezekiel 11:15). The exiles looked like people God had thrown away. Verse 5 reverses that judgment. The exiles are the good figs. Verse 6 turns the hard verbs of 1:10 into promises. God will build and plant them. Verse 7 adds a gift they could not make: a heart to know him.
The conqueror also comes under judgment

Verse 9 calls Babylon’s king “my servant.” Verse 12 says God will punish that king and nation. Being used by God is not the same as being approved. Babylon answers for its own wrongs. The seventy years set a limit of about a lifetime. The exile will be neither short nor endless. The cup in verses 18–26 starts with Jerusalem and ends with Babylon.
Earlier prophecy becomes evidence in a public hearing

The elders quote Micah 3:12 from about a century earlier (verse 18). Prophecies were remembered and could be cited in court. Verse 19 draws the precedent. Hezekiah feared the LORD, prayed, and the disaster did not come. So a warning of ruin is an invitation to change. Verses 20–23 add a second case with the opposite end. Uriah was killed, and one official saved Jeremiah (verse 24).
An object challenges the hope for immediate independence

Foreign envoys have gathered in Jerusalem (verse 3). They seem to be planning a revolt against Babylon. Jeremiah walks among them wearing a wooden yoke. Verse 12 gives the king his advice: serve Babylon and live. It sounds like disloyalty to his own country. His ground is in verses 5–6: the Creator has assigned this rule. Verse 7 adds that Babylon’s own time will also end.
Breaking a symbol does not settle a dispute

Both prophets speak in the LORD’s name in the same place. Jeremiah first wishes that Hananiah were right (verse 6). Verse 9 then gives the test. Earlier prophets warned of war, so a promise of peace must be proved. Time will show who was sent. Hananiah breaks the yoke, and Jeremiah simply leaves (verses 10–11). A dramatic act does not settle the dispute.
A promise of return includes ordinary life in exile

The letter names homes, gardens, marriages, and the city’s peace. Verse 7 asks the exiles to pray for Babylon, their captor. Their own welfare is bound up with that city’s welfare. Verse 5 uses “build” and “plant” from 1:10 for a foreign land. An Egyptian scribe’s palette shows the tools behind such a letter. The promise of verse 11 comes with a date of seventy years. Most who heard it would live out their lives in exile.
Healing answers both injury and exclusion

Verse 12 calls the wound incurable. Verse 14 says God himself struck the blow. Verse 17 then says the same God will heal it. The verse gives a reason drawn from an insult. Others called Zion an outcast that no one cares for. God answers the injury and the shame together. The one whom nobody seeks is sought by him.
The covenant promise changes where the law resides

The first covenant was written on stone tablets (Exodus 31:18). Chapter 17:1 said Judah’s sin was engraved on its heart. Verse 33 puts God’s law in that same place. Verse 32 says the people broke the earlier covenant. The new one changes where the law lives. Verse 34 rests it all on forgiveness. Hebrews 8:8–12 quotes this passage in full.
A land purchase gives hope a material form

The field lies in territory the enemy already controls. On any market it is worthless. Jeremiah still follows every legal step (verses 10–12). Verse 14 orders the deeds kept in a jar “that they may last many days.” The wait will be long. The purchase puts money behind the promise in verse 15. The tablet offers an earlier regional comparison for recording land sales.
Restoration receives the sounds of ordinary life

Three times Jeremiah said the bridegroom and bride would fall silent (7:34; 16:9). Verse 11 brings those very sounds back. Restoration is described in ordinary terms. People hold weddings and sing thanks in the LORD’s house. The song they sing is the refrain of Psalm 136. Verse 13 adds shepherds counting sheep. A healed land is one where daily life goes on.
A public promise loses meaning when power reverses it

Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12 required freedom after six years of service. The owners freed their slaves while the siege pressed them (verses 8–10). Verse 21 shows the army had pulled back for a time. Verse 16 says the owners then took the people back. They had sworn the release in the temple, so they profaned God’s name. A promise made under fear was dropped when the fear eased. Verse 17 turns their word “liberty” against them.
A family tradition creates a comparison, not a universal rule

Jonadab lived in the time of King Jehu, long before (2 Kings 10:15). His family still keeps his rules. Verse 14 sets that beside Judah’s record. God has spoken again and again, and Judah has not listened. The argument goes from the lesser to the greater. The LORD does not tell Judah to give up wine or houses. He praises the Rechabites’ loyalty, not their particular rules.
Destroying a copy does not end the message

The scroll moves through writing, public reading, court officials, and the king. Baruch writes it with ink (verse 18); a scribe’s palette held such ink. The officials tremble when they hear it (verse 16). The king cuts and burns it column by column (verse 23). Verse 24 notes that he did not tear his clothes. His father Josiah did tear his at a reading (2 Kings 22:11). Verse 32 says the second scroll was longer than the first.
A temporary change in the war encourages a false conclusion

The siege has lifted, and hope rises in the city. Verse 9 warns the people not to deceive themselves. The Babylonians “will not depart.” Verse 10 makes the point in an extreme form. Even an army of wounded men would rise and burn the city. A short change in the war proves nothing. Jeremiah’s advice to surrender also makes the desertion charge easy to believe (verse 13).
Practical care answers danger that official power created

The king gives Jeremiah up in verse 5, saying he can do nothing. A foreigner who serves in the palace acts in his place. Ebedmelech speaks to the king in public at the gate (verses 7–9). Verse 11 records where he found old rags and worn clothes. Verse 12 says they were to pad the ropes under Jeremiah’s arms. He thinks of a starved man’s skin. Chapter 39:15–18 gives him the LORD’s promise of safety.
The city's fall affects people in unequal ways

The chapter gives very different ends to different people. The king loses his sons and his sight (verses 6–7). The prophet is freed on Babylon’s orders (verses 11–14). The Ethiopian is promised his life (verses 16–18). Verse 10 says the poor, who owned nothing, received land. The text reports this and gives no motive for it. Jeremiah had charged the rich with seizing others’ goods (5:27–28; 22:13).
Harvest work offers a fragile recovery after conquest

Gedaliah’s plan in verse 10 is simple. He will deal with the Babylonians, and the people will farm. They should gather the harvest and live in their towns. Verses 11–12 show it working, as refugees return to a good crop. The recovery depends on one man. Verse 16 shows him refusing to believe a warning. In verses 2–3 a Babylonian officer states Jeremiah’s own message.
A local killing changes the survivors' political choices

The murder happens at a shared meal (verses 1–2). One killing ends the recovery described in chapter 40. Verse 18 gives the survivors’ reasoning. Babylon appointed Gedaliah, and Babylon will blame everyone for his death. Fear now drives their choices. Verse 5 shows pilgrims from the north still bringing offerings to a ruined temple. They are among the dead.
A promise to obey is tested by an unwanted answer

Verse 6 is a promise made before the answer is known. The people will obey “whether it is good, or whether it is bad.” They had already camped on the road to Egypt (41:17). Verse 7 makes them wait ten days. The answer goes against the plan they had formed. Verse 10 offers the building and planting of 1:10. Verse 20 says they misled themselves when they asked.
An accusation replaces an answer to the warning

The people promised to obey any answer (42:6). In verse 2 they call the answer a lie. Verse 3 gives their way out. They do not address the warning itself. They accuse the scribe Baruch of hidden motives. Blaming a third person lets them reject the message. Jeremiah is taken to the very place he warned against, and he keeps speaking there.
The dispute concerns the remembered cause of disaster

Both sides argue from the same events. The people say trouble began when they stopped their offerings (verse 18). Jeremiah says trouble came because they made them (verses 21–23). Each reads the past as proof. Verse 17 shows the people appealing to their fathers and kings. The dispute is about the remembered cause of a disaster. Verse 28 leaves the test to the outcome.
A scribe's private hopes meet a public crisis

Baruch came from a family of officials; his brother served the king (51:59). He could have hoped for a career. Verse 4 puts God’s own loss first. God is breaking down what he himself built and planted. Against that, verse 5 asks about Baruch’s private hopes. Personal ambition is out of scale in such a time. He is promised one thing: his life.
A river image exposes the gap between boast and outcome

The Nile’s yearly flood was Egypt’s strength and pride. Verse 8 uses it as a picture of the army. Egypt says it will rise and cover the earth. Verses 5–6 have already shown the soldiers running. The boast and the outcome stand side by side. Verse 17 gives Pharaoh a mocking nickname. Verse 26 still says Egypt will be inhabited again.
A question asks how long violence will continue

Verse 6 speaks to the sword itself. A voice asks how long before it will be quiet. It begs the sword to go back into its sheath. Verse 7 answers that it cannot rest while it has orders. The message is against an old enemy of Israel. It still contains a cry for the killing to stop. Verse 3 shows the cost: fathers who cannot help their children.
Grief remains beside the charge against Moab

Verse 29 states the charge against Moab: great pride. Verse 27 adds that it laughed at Israel. Then verse 31 says, “I will wail for Moab.” The voice that judges also mourns. Verse 36 says the speaker’s heart moans like a flute. Judgment and grief come from the same mouth. Verse 47 ends the chapter with a promise of restoration.
Different neighbors receive different endings

Each people in this chapter relied on something different. Ammon had treasure and fertile valleys (verse 4). Edom had wisdom and cliffs (verses 7 and 16). Damascus had fame, Kedar had distance, and Elam had the bow. Every one of these protections fails. The endings are not the same. Ammon and Elam are restored, and Edom’s orphans are kept (verses 6, 11, 39).
Being used in judgment does not excuse violence

Verse 7 quotes the enemies’ defense. Israel sinned against the LORD, so those who devoured it are “not guilty.” They borrow the prophets’ own teaching to excuse themselves. The chapter rejects that excuse. Verse 11 says Babylon rejoiced as it plundered. Verse 29 says it was proud against the LORD. Being the means of judgment did not make its cruelty innocent.
Reading and sinking make a message into a witnessed act

Verse 59 dates this to Zedekiah’s fourth year. In that same period Jeremiah told the exiles to pray for Babylon (29:7). The exiles should seek the city’s peace, and its fall is already written. Jeremiah wrote this in a book (verse 60); the palette shows a scribe’s tools. Seraiah is to read the scroll aloud in Babylon. A stone then sends the scroll beneath the river’s surface. Verse 64 explains the act: Babylon will sink and not rise.
The appendix keeps a surviving king beside an unrepaired loss

Chapter 51:64 said Jeremiah’s words ended there. This chapter adds history that matches 2 Kings 25. It shows that the city fell as he had said. Verses 17–23 list the temple’s bronze piece by piece as it is taken. Nothing is said to repair that loss. Verse 31 then reports a small mercy to a captive king. The book ends with a ruined temple and a living heir of David.
